title: Incidence of Infectious Diseases in Bulgaria over a 50-Year Period (1974–2023)
content: Objective: To investigate the long-term trends and dynamics of acute infectious diseases morbidity in Bulgaria across half of century of significant socio-economic transitions, healthcare reforms, and geopolitical integrations. Methods: retrospective epidemiological study was conducted covering a 50-year period (1974–2023). Aggregated data from 10 consecutive five-year cohorts were extracted from official statutory reporting networks managed by the National Statistical Institute (NSI), the National Center for Public Health and Analyses (NCPHA), and the National Center for Infectious and Parasitic Diseases (NCIPD). Results: Drastic shifts in infectious disease dynamics correlate directly with national immunization strategies, economic transitions, and the entry into force of healthcare reforms. Mass immunoprophylaxis achieved successful elimination patterns or historic minimums for core respiratory and neuro-invasive pathogens, including diphtheria and rubella. However, recent 2020-2023 metrics reveal sub-optimal measles-mumpsrubella (MMR) and pertussis coverage, sparking a notable upward trend in pertussis morbidity and infant mortality. Pathogens lacking mass vaccination frameworks, such as varicella and scarlet fever, exhibited sharp post-pandemic resurgences following the relaxation of containment measures. Climate-driven shifts are expanding vector-borne footprints, such as West Nile fever. Furthermore, the COVID-19 pandemic introduced substantial diagnostic reporting artefacts and a heavy excess mortality burden. Conclusions: Long-term surveillance data confirms a persistent overall decline in vaccine-preventable diseases alongside expanding relative shares of intestinal, emerging vector-borne, and non-vaccine-preventable respiratory infections. Tracking these dynamics provides a vital public health baseline for mitigating vaccine hesitancy and changing ecological disease boundaries.
